stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield. They have 40 garden plots available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of commute time (minutes) are:

**City A:** 17, 18, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 22, 24, 26, 27, 27, 29, 30, 30

**City B:** 15, 16, 26, 26, 27, 28, 30, 30, 31, 31, 32, 33, 33, 42, 65

A random sample of 17 students at a large school reported hours of sleep on a school night: x̄ = 7.86 hours, s = 0.93 hours. A dotplot of the data shows no strong skew or outliers. A health report claims students at the school sleep 8.6 hours on average.

Data were collected on outdoor temperature (°F) (x) and daily iced-drink sales (y) for a sample of days. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    57.8
x           3.4
S = 2    R-Sq = 63.0%
```

questions.stem: For a distribution of household incomes in a city, the mean is 52 and the median is 59. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.

questions.explanation: Mean 52 < median 59: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: The data are: 12, 17, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 28, 35, 37, 38, 64. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 17.5, Q3 = 36; values above 48.3 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 17.5, Q3 = 36; values above 54.5 are outliers, so 64 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

options.text: Q1 = 17.5, Q3 = 36; values above 63.8 are outliers, so 64 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 18.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 63.8.

questions.stem: For a distribution of number of social media followers, the mean is 41 and the median is 49. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.

questions.explanation: Mean 41 < median 49: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: In an experiment on a new reading program, students are first grouped by reading level, then randomly assigned to programs within each level. What is the purpose of grouping by level?

options.why: It remains an experiment.
Groups by level are not placebo groups.

options.text: Blocking, to reduce variability caused by reading level
options.why: Correct. Blocking controls a known source of variation.
That is a sampling idea.

questions.explanation: Blocking controls a known source of variation.

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean

questions.stem: Each of 3 independent devices fails with probability 0.05. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: That is the probability all fail.
Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
That is the probability none fail.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 170 customers of an online store, 83 would recommend it to a friend. Which is a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all customers of an online store who would recommend it to a friend?

options.why: Use z* for 90%, not 1.96.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.645.
Divide by n inside the square root.

questions.stem: The data are: 10, 11, 11, 13, 17, 20, 22, 22, 24, 25, 26, 62. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 12, Q3 = 24.5; values above 39.8 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

options.text: Q1 = 12, Q3 = 24.5; values above 43.3 are outliers, so 62 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 12.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 43.3.

options.text: Q1 = 12, Q3 = 24.5; values above 37 are outliers, so 62 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior) overall.
That is P(drives | junior).
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.

questions.stem: As degrees of freedom increase, what happens to the t distribution?

options.why: They get lighter.
Its mean stays 0.
t is symmetric.

options.text: It approaches the standard normal distribution
options.why: Correct. Tails become lighter.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 47, s₁ = 16 and n₂ = 56, s₂ = 11. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Variances add, even for a difference.
Each sample contributes s²/n.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 220 teenagers in a state, 101 get at least 8 hours of sleep. Which is a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in a state who get at least 8 hours of sleep?

options.why: Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 2.576.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Divide by n inside the square root.
Use z* for 99%, not 1.96.

questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in with their opinions about a new law. Which type of bias is most likely?

options.why: The question wording is not the main issue.
The main problem is self-selection.

options.text: No bias, because listeners chose freely
options.why: Self-selection causes bias.
Correct. People with strong opinions are more likely to call.

questions.explanation: People with strong opinions are more likely to call.

questions.stem: Each of 20 students takes a reading test before and after a summer program. Which procedure compares the scores?

options.why: The samples are not independent.
Scores are quantitative.

options.text: A paired t procedure on the differences (after − before)
options.why: Correct. Two measurements on the same students are paired.
That is for categorical data.

questions.explanation: Two measurements on the same students are paired.

questions.stem: What is the expected value of X?

options.why: Weight each value by its probability.
That is the largest probability, not the mean.
Correct. μ = Σ x·P(x).
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.2 and P(A and B) = 0.1. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.
Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.08.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.08.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior) overall.
Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.
That is P(drives | junior).
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.

questions.stem: The correlation between car age and resale price is r = 0.95. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 95% of the variation in resale price is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

options.text: About 90.3% of the variation in resale price is accounted for by the linear model relating resale price to car age
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

options.text: Car age causes 90.3% of resale price
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 90.3% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

options.why: Variances add, even for a difference.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Each sample contributes s²/n.

options.text: Q1 = 17.5, Q3 = 37; values above 61.3 are outliers

questions.stem: Each of 15 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.1. What is the probability of at most 5 successes?

options.why: That is only P(X = k).
That is the complement.
Correct. Use the binomial distribution with n = 15 and p = 0.1.
That is P(X < k); 'at most k' includes k.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.05 at 95% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Square z*/m.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 1.96, rounded up.
Always round up to guarantee the margin.

questions.stem: A random sample of 27 gives x̄ = 119.6 and s = 20. Test H₀: μ = 125 versus Hₐ: μ < 125. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Divide by the standard error s/√n.
The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.

questions.stem: The slope of a regression line predicting exam score from hours studied is 3.5. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: For each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by about 3.5 points
options.why: Correct. Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

options.text: A student who studies 0 hours scores 3.5
options.why: That would be the intercept.

options.text: 35% of the variation in scores is explained
options.why: That is r².

options.text: Each student's score increases by exactly 3.5 points per hour
options.why: The slope describes predicted, not actual, values.

questions.explanation: Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.2 versus Hₐ: p > 0.2, a random sample of 300 gives p̂ = 0.27. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.
The alternative is one-sided.
The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.

questions.stem: A random sample of 15 gives x̄ = 102.5 and s = 23. Test H₀: μ = 115 versus Hₐ: μ < 115. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
Divide by the standard error s/√n.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.

questions.stem: A population has mean 85 and standard deviation 15 (shape unknown). For random samples of 100, what is the approximate probability that the sample mean exceeds 87.3?

options.why: Divide σ by √n, not n.
Correct. By the CLT, x̄ is approximately normal with SD 15/√100 = 1.5.
Use σ/√n for a sample mean.
That is the area below.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 77 and standard deviation 16. What proportion of values are less than 59.4?

options.why: That is the other side of the boundary.
Divide by σ when standardizing.
Use the normal distribution's area, not the z-score.

questions.stem: A random sample of 39 has mean 29.8 and standard deviation 12.8. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the population mean?

options.why: Divide s by √n.
Divide by √n, not n.
With s estimating σ, use t*, not z*.
Correct. x̄ ± t*·s/√n with t* = 2.024 (df = 38).

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.7 versus Hₐ: p > 0.7, a random sample of 260 gives p̂ = 0.72. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The test's standard deviation uses p₀, not p̂.
The alternative is one-sided.
Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.

questions.stem: For a set of data, x̄ = 19, sx = 7, ȳ = 159, sy = 33 and r = -0.6. What is the least-squares regression line?

options.why: a = ȳ − b·x̄.
The slope is r·sy/sx, not r·sx/sy.
Correct. b = r·sy/sx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Multiply sy/sx by r.

questions.stem: Researchers randomly selected 200 customers of the store and asked which of two study apps they already use, then compared test scores. Can the researchers conclude that the app causes higher scores, and to whom do the results apply?

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, and yes to generalizing to all customers of the store
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: No to cause and effect, but the association can be generalized to all customers of the store
options.why: Correct. No random assignment decides causation; random selection decides generalization.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, but only for the volunteers in the study
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: No to cause and effect, and no generalization beyond the volunteers
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

questions.explanation: Random assignment: no. Random selection: yes.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 26, s₁ = 11 and n₂ = 45, s₂ = 11. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Variances add, even for a difference.
Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Each sample contributes s²/n.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 18 + 1.4x. An observation has x = 20 and y = 50. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: 4; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: -4; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.

options.text: 4; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.

questions.stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p > 0.4 gives a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: There is a 0.03 probability that H₀ is true
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of a hypothesis.
Unrelated to the p-value.

options.text: There is a 0.97 probability that Hₐ is true
options.why: Not a valid interpretation.

options.text: If p = 0.4, there is a 0.03 probability of a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed, by chance alone
options.why: Correct. That is the definition of the p-value.

questions.explanation: That is the definition of the p-value.

questions.stem: X and Y are independent with μX = 11, σX = 5, μY = 34, σY = 2. What are the mean and standard deviation of X − Y?

options.why: Standard deviations do not add; variances do.
That is the variance; take the square root.
Correct. Means add or subtract; variances add.
Check the sign of the mean.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.03 at 99% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 2.576, rounded up.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Square z*/m.
Always round up to guarantee the margin.

questions.stem: Assuming the null hypothesis of a chi-square test is true, what is the expected count for Group 1, Option A?

options.why: Divide by the table total once.
Correct. Expected = (row total × column total) / table total.
That is the observed count.
Expected counts depend on the row and column totals.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 90 of 300 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 43 of 120 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Divide the difference by its standard error.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.3167; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 39 of 140 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 59 of 160 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.3267; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
Divide the difference by its standard error.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.

questions.stem: For a chi-square test of homogeneity on these counts, what are the test statistic and degrees of freedom?

options.why: Do not take a square root.
For a two-way table, df = (r − 1)(c − 1).
Correct. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E with df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).
Do not divide by the total.

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the new fertilizer lead to a better total weight of tomatoes harvested than the standard fertilizer for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the new fertilizer vs the standard fertilizer). Response: total weight of tomatoes harvested.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 40 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–40; use a random number generator to select 20 different numbers.
Those 20 receive the new fertilizer; the remaining 20 receive the standard fertilizer.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by sun exposure (full sun or partial shade). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by sun exposure.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether City B has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 7; upper fence = 33 + 1.5(7) = 43.5. Outlier(s): 65.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for City B (30) is greater than for City A (22).
City B is less variable (IQR 7 vs 8).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: City B has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for City B, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 31 is pulled toward the high value; median 30 is not.

parts.prompt: Identify the procedure and check the conditions for a 95% confidence interval for the mean.

rubric.criterion: One-sample t interval; random, 10%, and normality justified by the dotplot (n under 30).
rubric.example: n = 17; the sample shows no strong skew or outliers.

rubric.criterion: Confidence in capturing the population mean.
rubric.example: We are 95% confident that the interval from 7.38 to 8.35 hours captures the true mean hours of sleep for students at the school.

parts.prompt: Does the interval support the report's claim? Explain.

rubric.example: 8.6 is outside the interval, so it is not plausible; the data contradict the claim.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 57.8 + 3.4x, where ŷ is predicted daily iced-drink sales and x is outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of outdoor temperature (°F), the predicted daily iced-drink sales increases by about 3.4.
About 63.0% of the variation in daily iced-drink sales is accounted for by the linear model with outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 10 and y = 96.1. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 91.8; residual = 96.1 − 91.8 = 4.3: the actual value is above the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of days from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
